### __q1__ Planning a study (TEAMWORK)

While you provided this plan in c08 (Part 1), please include your plan here. In particular, describe how you updated your plan in response to feedback.

#### Population

- (What population are you going to study?)
  - We are going to study students at Arcadia University, across all majors, that do not       play piano.

#### Quantity of interest

- (Write your quantity of interest here)
  - Our quantity of interest is results from the attention test.

#### Covariates

- The type of music - we are going to be making people listen to classical music.
- Majors are a covariate, but we are going to be studying students from every major and      selecting randomly. 
- Age - we found that there was a wide range of ages in the university, so we tracked it to   see if it had an effect on scores.
- Whether people usually listen to classical music or not - we don't expect this to effect   anything, but we will be tracking this just in case.

#### Observation or experiment?

The Islands allows you to ask islanders to complete tasks. If you just take measurements on your participants, then it's an *observational study*. But if you also introduce something that's meant to change the outcome of a measurement (e.g., drinking coffee before taking a test), that's called an *experimental study*. You need to decide whether your study is observational or experimental.

- This is going to be an experimental study. We are going to make people listen to music or   play an instrument before taking an attention test to see the effect of the actions.

#### Question / Hypothesis

- Does actively playing music or passively listening to music improve attention span? If     so, does one improve it more than the other?
- We have a control group to ensure that scores don't just improve because people are        retaking the test. We hypothesized that actively playing or listening to music will        improve attention span and that both will have a relatively similar effect.

#### Sampling plan

- (What steps will you take to collect the data?)
  - Be specific. For instance, if you're going to collect a random sample, how will you enumerate all of the things to be sampled?
  - Write a protocol. Document step-by-step instructions that your team will follow. That way, you can feasibly split up data collection among the whole team, while making sure each team member doesn't make ad hoc decisions that introduce bias into your results.
  
1. Copy a list of students at Arcadia University onto a Google Document and make the list numbered.
2. Use a random number generator to select 75 numbers. Find the students corresponding with those numbers on the list.
3. Ask each student what instruments they play.
4. If the student says they play piano, generate a new random number and find a new person. Ask them the same thing and ensure they do not play piano. Make sure to keep track of the numbers of students who have been removed from the study so we don't go back to them.
5. Once we have a desirable set of people, split the students into 3 groups of 25. 
6. Ask each person if they listen to classical music or not. Record their answer to this question, their age, and their major.
7. Give the first group an attention test. Record their score and wait 10 minutes before giving them an attention test again. Record the new score.
8. Give the second group an attention test. Record their score and make them listen to classical music for 10 minutes before giving them an attention test again. Record the new score.
9. Give the third group an attention test. Record their score and make them play piano for 10 minutes before giving them an attention test again. Record the new score.
10. Repeat steps 7-9 over two more days. 

- (How will you ensure the data is representative of your chosen population?)
  - We we will take a random sample of the students that does not depend on major, so that     the group is representative of the whole university. We will ask everyone what             instruments they play to ensure no one we're studying plays piano. 
  
- (For experiments only: How will you ensure any effects you observe are due to the treatment, and not due to other factors?)
  - We will take an attention test six times across three different days. This gives us        more data that can combat differences in attention that may be due to day-to-day           factors like mood or weather.

- (How will you choose your sample size?)
  - We chose a sample size of 25 per group because it would be a reasonable amount of data     to collect, while also giving us fairly accurate results. With a sample group of 25, a     target power of 75%, and a significance level of 10%,  we have a minimum detectable        Cohen's f of about 0.3, which will allow us to find medium-sized effects.
  
Based on the feedback we received, we made sure to check our sample size in terms of the accuracy it could achieve, and we confirmed it would give us a result we were comfortable with. We also made our sampling plan more specific so it is clear that we do have a control group.

```{r}
data <- data %>%
  group_by(Major) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    names_to = "Attention Test Number",
    values_to = "Number Missed",
    cols = contains("Attention")
    ) %>%
  mutate(
    `Attention Test Number` = str_extract(`Attention Test Number`, "\\d") %>%
      as.integer()
    )

mean_by_test <- data %>%
  group_by(`Attention Test Number`, Day, Group) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_missed = mean(`Number Missed`, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    Test_no = (Day - 1) * 2 + `Attention Test Number`,
    ) %>%
  arrange(Group, Test_no)

mean_by_test

mean_by_test %>%
  ggplot(aes(Test_no, `mean_missed`, color = Group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

### __q4__ Answers

Connect your Key Analyses to your questions / hypotheses. What did you conclude from your study?

We concluded that playing piano and passively listening to music improve attention span, but playing piano causes a greater improvement. A positive score change indicates that someone did worse and missed more markers on an attention test the second time they took it, while a negative score change indicates that they did better. Over all 3 days, the median score change of the control group was positive. On the other hand, both the median score changes for the playing piano and passively listening to music groups were negative. The playing piano group had the lowest median, meaning people in that group generally had the greatest improvements in score out of all the groups.

Interestingly, we also found that the results for the listening to music group were much different on day 3 than on other days. Our second graph compares the results to each individual test over all 3 days, and there is a large dip in scores for the listening group for the second test on day 3. Before, the scores had been much more consistent across each test than in the other groups. While the overall trend in our data indicates that playing piano causes the greatest improvement in attention span, it should be noted that day-to-day differences such as mood can also play a role in people's attention levels.

When initially creating our experiment, we expected that colleges in the Islands have a similar population to Olin where almost all of the students are in the 17-22 age range. However, the Islands have a much more diverse age population at Arcadia University. Since we hadn't initially planned on tracking this, we wanted to see if age was affecting data at all. Fortunately, the plot shows that age doesn't play a concrete role in how well students were doing on the attention tests. As shown by the graph, different groups display different trends when it comes to age. The listening group shows that participants perform worse as they get older, but the playing piano group shows that participants perform better as they get older. This graph also does show that playing music increases attention. The line we fitted to the piano group is below the line we fitted to the control group.
